summary.text: For a positive finite set with \(s\) relevant primes, the proof organizes the \(p\)-adic valuations and residue signs into weighted laminar cancellation trees whose opposition kernel is \(\log((a+b)/\gcd(a,b))\), with a two-adic correction; this kernel is conditionally negative semidefinite, while the associated signed kernel is bounded off the diagonal by \(\log(|a-b|/(a+b))<0\). Energy estimates, laminar pruning, and an almost-obtuse sign-vector packing bound then give \(|A|\le 1024(s+1)^8\); removing a possible zero and applying this to an extremal set yields polynomial growth of \(f(n)\), hence \(f(n)/\log n\to\infty\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(A)=\left|\left\{p\text{ prime}:p\mid a+b\text{ for some distinct }a,b\in A\right\}\right|.
\]
This is exactly the number of distinct prime divisors of the ordered off-diagonal product
\(\prod_{a\ne b\in A}(a+b)\): a prime divides that product if and only if it divides at least one of its factors. We shall prove the following quantitative statement.

**Quantitative assertion.** If \(A\) is a finite set of positive integers and \(s=c(A)\), then
\[
 |A|\le 1024(s+1)^8. \tag{1}
\]

Once (1) is established, the desired asymptotic result follows fairly directly. The main work is therefore the proof of (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Laminar opposition families

We first formulate an abstract finite combinatorial result.

Let \(I\) be a finite set. A weighted laminar family on \(I\) consists of a finite collection \(\mathcal L\) of subsets of \(I\), with nonnegative weights \(w(B)\), such that any two members are nested or disjoint. Its kernel is
\[
 U(i,j)=\sum_{\substack{B\in\mathcal L\\i,j\in B}}w(B).
\]
It is positive semidefinite, because for every real vector \(q=(q_i)_{i\in I}\),
\[
 \sum_{i,j}q_iq_jU(i,j)
 =\sum_{B\in\mathcal L}w(B)\left(\sum_{i\in B}q_i\right)^2\ge0. \tag{2}
\]

An opposition family is such a laminar family together with signs
\(\varepsilon(i)\in\{1,-1\}\), subject to the condition that every member of \(\mathcal L\) is bichromatic: it contains both signs. Define
\[
 S(i,j)=\varepsilon(i)\varepsilon(j)U(i,j),
\]
\[
 O(i,j)=\begin{cases}U(i,j),&\varepsilon(i)\ne\varepsilon(j),\\0,&\varepsilon(i)=\varepsilon(j),\end{cases}
\quad
 A(i,j)=\begin{cases}U(i,j),&\varepsilon(i)=\varepsilon(j),\\0,&\varepsilon(i)\ne\varepsilon(j).
\end{cases}
\]
Thus
\[
 S=A-O,\qquad U=A+O,\qquad O=\frac{U-S}{2}. \tag{3}
\]
The signed kernel \(S\) is also positive semidefinite, by applying (2) to \(q_i\varepsilon(i)\).

Suppose now that we have \(s\) opposition families, indexed by a finite set \(P\). Write their kernels as \(U_p,S_p,O_p,A_p\), and put
\[
 U=\sum_{p\in P}U_p,\qquad V=\sum_{p\in P}S_p,
 \qquad D=\sum_{p\in P}O_p.
\]
We use the quadratic-form notation
\(Q_K(q)=\sum_{i,j}q_iq_jK(i,j)\). A symmetric kernel \(D\) with zero diagonal is called conditionally negative semidefinite if
\[
 \sum_iq_i=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_D(q)\le0. \tag{4}
\]

The abstract result we need is this.

**Opposition-capacity lemma.** Assume

1. \(V(i,j)<0\) whenever \(i\ne j\);
2. \(D\) is conditionally negative semidefinite.

Then
\[
 |I|\le 1024(s+1)^8. \tag{5}
\]

We give the full proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Energy and diameter estimates

Let
\[
 L=\max_{i,j\in I}D(i,j).
\]
The cases where \(I\) is very small will later be disposed of immediately. In the remaining case \(|I|>1\), one has \(L>0\). Indeed, take distinct \(i,j\). Since \(U(i,j)\ge0\), (3) gives
\[
 D(i,j)=\frac{U(i,j)-V(i,j)}2>0.
\]

We first obtain an energy estimate for every individual unsigned kernel \(U_p\). Since every set in the \(p\)-th laminar family is bichromatic, for each \(i\) there is some \(j\) such that
\[
 U_p(i,i)=O_p(i,j).
\]
To see this, choose the smallest laminar set containing \(i\). It is contained in every other set containing \(i\), and by bichromaticity contains an oppositely signed \(j\). Thus every set counted by \(U_p(i,i)\) also contains \(j\). If no laminar set contains \(i\), both sides are zero. Consequently
\[
 U_p(i,i)\le L,
\quad	ext{and hence}\quad
U(i,i)\le sL. \tag{6}
\]
Also \(V(i,i)=U(i,i)\).

We shall use the elementary fact that if a positive semidefinite kernel \(K\) has nonpositive off-diagonal entries, then
\[
 Q_K(q)\le 2\sum_i q_i^2K(i,i). \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, apply positive semidefiniteness to \((|q_i|)\). For \(i\ne j\),
\((q_iq_j+|q_iq_j|)K(i,j)\le0\), while on the diagonal this expression is \(2q_i^2K(i,i)\). Summing gives
\(Q_K(q)+Q_K(|q|)\le2\sum_iq_i^2K(i,i)\), and \(Q_K(|q|)\ge0\).

For a zero-sum vector \(q\), conditional negative definiteness and (3) give
\[
0\ge Q_D(q)=\frac{Q_U(q)-Q_V(q)}2,
\]
so \(Q_U(q)\le Q_V(q)\). The kernel \(V\) is positive semidefinite, and by assumption its off-diagonal entries are negative. Thus (7) and (6) imply, for each \(p\),
\[
 Q_{U_p}(q)\le Q_U(q)\le Q_V(q)
 \le 2sL\sum_iq_i^2. \tag{8}
\]
The first inequality holds because \(U-U_p\) is a sum of positive semidefinite kernels.

We also need a diameter estimate. Laminarity gives the ultrametric-similarity inequality
\[
 \min\{U_p(x,i),U_p(x,j)\}\le U_p(i,j). \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, if every laminar set containing \(x,i\) also contains \(j\), then the first term is at most \(U_p(i,j)\). Otherwise choose a set containing \(x,i\) but not \(j\); laminarity then forces every set containing \(x,j\) to contain \(i\), giving the inequality for the second term.

Accounting for signs, (9) implies
\[
 \min\{O_p(x,i),O_p(x,j)\}\le A_p(i,j). \tag{10}
\]
If one of \(i,j\) has the same sign as \(x\), one term on the left is zero. Otherwise \(i,j\) have the same sign and (10) is exactly (9). Moreover, for distinct \(i,j\),
\[
 A_p(i,j)<D(i,j), \tag{11}
\]
because
\[
V(i,j)=\sum_p A_p(i,j)-D(i,j)<0

after summing agreements, and every agreement is nonnegative.

Let \(T\subseteq I\) satisfy \(D(i,j)\le\delta\) for all \(i,j\in T\). For fixed \(x,p\), there is at most one \(y\in T\) with \(O_p(x,y)>\delta\). Otherwise two such points \(i,j\) would, by (10), satisfy
\(A_p(i,j)>\delta\), contradicting (11) and \(D(i,j)\le\delta\).

Thus, if \(|T|>2s\), then for any \(a,b\in I\) we can choose \(y\in T\) avoiding all the at most \(s\) exceptional points for \(a\) and all the at most \(s\) exceptional points for \(b\). It follows that
\[
D(a,y)=\sum_pO_p(a,y)\le s\delta,
\qquad D(b,y)\le s\delta. \tag{12}
\]
Finally, conditional negative definiteness gives
\[
D(a,b)\le2D(a,y)+2D(b,y). \tag{13}
\]
This follows by applying (4) to the zero-sum vector
\(e_a+e_b-2e_y\), using symmetry and the zero diagonal. Combining (12) and (13),
\[
 D(a,b)\le4s\delta. \tag{14}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Pruning one laminar family

We next prove a pruning statement from the energy bound (8).

Let \(U\) be a nonnegative weighted laminar kernel on an \(N\)-point set, and suppose
\[
 Q_U(q)\le M\sum_iq_i^2\qquad\text{whenever }\sum_iq_i=0. \tag{15}
\]
Fix an integer \(t\ge2\) with \(2t<N\).

Call \(j\) a small neighbor of \(i\) if some laminar set of cardinality less than \(t\) contains both. All small laminar sets containing a fixed point form a chain, so their union is their largest member. Therefore each point has at most \(t\) small neighbors, and this neighbor relation is symmetric.

Consider a chain \(\mathcal C\) of laminar sets lying between sets \(C\subseteq D\), where
\(|C|\ge t\) and \(|I\setminus D|\ge t\). Define the zero-sum contrast
\[
q_i=\frac{1_C(i)}{|C|}-\frac{1_{I\setminus D}(i)}{|I\setminus D|}.
\]
The supports are disjoint, and hence
\[
 \sum_iq_i^2=\frac1{|C|}+\frac1{|I\setminus D|}\le\frac2t. \tag{16}
\]
For every member \(B\) of the chain between \(C\) and \(D\), one has
\(\sum_{i\in B}q_i=1\). Expanding the laminar energy as in (2), and retaining only these nonnegative terms, (15) and (16) yield
\[
 \sum_{B\in\mathcal C}w(B)\le\frac{2M}{t}. \tag{17}
\]

The sets of size greater than \(N-t\) form a chain: two disjoint such sets would have total size greater than \(N\). Let \(Z\) be the complement of the smallest one, or the empty set if no such set exists. Then \(|Z|<t\), and every set of size greater than \(N-t\) contains every point outside \(Z\). Let
\[
 \beta=\sum_{|B|>N-t}w(B)\ge0.
\]
If \(i,j\notin Z\) are distinct and are not small neighbors, the common laminar sets containing both and having size at most \(N-t\) form a chain. Its smallest member has size at least \(t\), since \(i,j\) are not small neighbors, and the complement of its largest possible upper endpoint has size at least \(t\). Therefore (17) applies. The sets larger than \(N-t\) contribute exactly \(\beta\), and all remaining common sets contribute between \(0\) and \(2M/t\). Thus
\[
 \beta\le U(i,j)\le\beta+\frac{2M}{t}. \tag{18}
\]

In summary, pruning supplies a set \(Z\) of at most \(t\) points, a symmetric forbidden-neighbor relation of degree at most \(t\), and a baseline \(\beta\ge0\), such that (18) holds outside \(Z\) and the forbidden relation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Almost-obtuse sign vectors

We need one more elementary estimate. Let \(P\) have cardinality \(s\), let \(\beta_p\ge0\), and assign to every vertex \(i\) signs \(\varepsilon_p(i)\in\{1,-1\}\). Put
\[
 G(i,j)=\sum_p\beta_p\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_p(j),
 \qquad B=\sum_p\beta_p.
\]
If \(B>0\) and
\[
 2sG(i,j)\le B\qquad(i\ne j), \tag{19}
\]
then the number \(m\) of vertices is at most \(4s\).

Here is an elementary proof. First,
\[
 \sum_{i,j}G(i,j)=\sum_p\beta_p\left(\sum_i\varepsilon_p(i)\right)^2\ge0. \tag{20}
\]
Also, expanding squares and retaining the terms with equal feature indices gives
\[
 \sum_{i,j}G(i,j)^2
 =\sum_{p,q}\beta_p\beta_q
   \left(\sum_i\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_q(i)\right)^2
 \ge m^2\sum_p\beta_p^2.
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz, \(B^2\le s\sum_p\beta_p^2\), so
\[
 m^2B^2\le s\sum_{i,j}G(i,j)^2. \tag{21}
\]
For every entry, \(G(i,j)\ge-B\). Consider
\[
 F(x)=(x+B)(2sx-B).
\]
For an off-diagonal entry, both \(x+B\ge0\) and, by (19), \(2sx-B\le0\), so \(F(G(i,j))\le0\). On the diagonal \(G(i,i)=B\), and \(F(B)\le4sB^2\). Hence
\[
 \sum_{i,j}F(G(i,j))\le4smB^2. \tag{22}
\]
On expanding the left side,
\[
\sum F(G)=2s\sum G^2+(2s-1)B\sum G-m^2B^2.
\]
The middle term is nonnegative by (20). Combining this with (21) and (22) gives
\(m^2B^2\le4smB^2\). Since \(m>0\) and \(B>0\), this yields \(m\le4s\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Proof of the opposition-capacity lemma

Set
\[
 t=64(s+1)^4.
\]
If \(|I|\le2t\), then immediately
\(|I|\le1024(s+1)^8\). Assume henceforth that \(|I|>2t\). As above, \(L>0\), and the energy bound (8) holds with
\[
 M=2sL.
\]
Apply the pruning result separately to every \(U_p\). We obtain exceptional sets \(Z_p\), forbidden relations \(\sim_p\), and baselines \(\beta_p\ge0\), with
\[
 |Z_p|\le t,\qquad \deg(\sim_p)\le t,

a nd, outside these exceptions,
\[
 \beta_p\le U_p(i,j)\le\beta_p+r,
 \qquad r=\frac{2M}{t}. \tag{23}
\]
Let
\[
 Z=\bigcup_pZ_p,
 \qquad i\sim j\iff i\sim_pj\text{ for some }p,
 \qquad Y=I\setminus Z.
\]
Then
\[
 |Z|\le st,
 \qquad \deg(\sim)\le st. \tag{24}
\]
Put
\[
 e=sr,\qquad B=\sum_p\beta_p.

a
\]
(The stray letter in the preceding display has no mathematical role; the definition is simply \(e=sr\) and \(B=\sum_p\beta_p\).) With the chosen value of \(t\), direct cancellation gives
\[
 16s^2e
 =16s^2\cdot s\frac{4sL}{64(s+1)^4}
 \le L, \tag{25}
\]
since \(s^4\le(s+1)^4\).

Let \(T\subseteq Y\) contain no distinct forbidden pair. Then (23) holds for every distinct \(i,j\in T\) and every \(p\). It follows that
\[
 D(i,j)\le B+e. \tag{26}
\]
Indeed, each \(O_p(i,j)\) is either zero or \(U_p(i,j)\le\beta_p+r\).

Furthermore, multiplication by signs changes an approximation by at most the same error. More precisely, from (23),
\[
 \beta_p\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_p(j)
 \le S_p(i,j)+r.

a
\]
Summing and using \(V(i,j)<0\) gives, for distinct \(i,j\in T\),
\[
G(i,j)=\sum_p\beta_p\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_p(j)<e. \tag{27}
\]

We claim that \(|T|\le4s\). This is immediate if \(|T|\le2s\). Otherwise apply the diameter bound (14), using (26), to a pair \(a,b\) attaining the global maximum \(D(a,b)=L\). We get
\[
 L\le4s(B+e). \tag{28}
\]
Together, (25) and (28) imply
\[
 2se\le B. \tag{29}
\]
For completeness, if \(B=0\), (29) forces \(e=0\), and then (28) contradicts \(L>0\); hence \(B>0\). One can derive (29) directly by dividing (25) by \(4s\) and comparing with (28); the inequalities \(s\ge1\) and \(e\ge0\) account for the harmless slack. Now (27) and (29) imply
\[
 2sG(i,j)\le2se\le B
\]
for distinct \(i,j\). The almost-obtuse sign-vector estimate therefore gives \(|T|\le4s\), as claimed.

Choose a maximal subset \(T\subseteq Y\) containing no forbidden pair. Maximality says that every point of \(Y\) is either in \(T\) or is a forbidden neighbor of some point of \(T\). Since every forbidden neighborhood has at most \(st\) points,
\[
 |Y|\le |T|(st+1)\le4s(st+1). \tag{30}
\]
Combining (24) and (30),
\[
 |I|\le st+4s(st+1). \tag{31}
\]
With \(t=64(s+1)^4\), elementary expansion and the inequalities
\(s\le(s+1)^2\), \(s^2\le(s+1)^2\), and
\((s+1)^6\le(s+1)^8\) give
\[
 st+4s(st+1)\le1024(s+1)^8.
\]
This proves the opposition-capacity lemma.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. The logarithmic kernel

We now construct the opposition families arising from positive integers.

We first record the analytic input. For positive reals \(a_i\), the kernel
\[
 K_0(i,j)=\log(a_i+a_j)
\]
is conditionally negative semidefinite. To prove this, set
\[
 r_i=\frac{a_i-1}{a_i+1},
\]
so \(|r_i|<1\), and note the identity
\[
\log(a_i+a_j)=\log(a_i+1)+\log(a_j+1)-\log2
 +\log(1-r_ir_j). \tag{32}
\]
For a zero-sum vector \(q\), the first three terms in (32) contribute zero to the quadratic form. On the other hand,
\[
 -\log(1-r_ir_j)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{r_i^nr_j^n}{n},

a
\]
and hence
\[
 \sum_{i,j}q_iq_j[-\log(1-r_ir_j)]
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n\left(\sum_iq_ir_i^n\right)^2\ge0.
\]
Thus the quadratic form of \(\log(a_i+a_j)\) is nonpositive on zero-sum vectors.

Two further kernels are positive semidefinite. First,
\[
 (i,j)\longmapsto \log\gcd(a_i,a_j)

a
\]
is positive semidefinite. Indeed, the divisor expansion
\[
 \log\gcd(a_i,a_j)
 =\sum_{d\mid a_i,\ d\mid a_j}\Lambda(d)

a
\]
expresses it as a nonnegative weighted sum of rank-one kernels
\(1_{d\mid a_i}1_{d\mid a_j}\), because the von Mangoldt weights \(\Lambda(d)\) are nonnegative. Second, for any labeling \(\ell_i\), the equivalence kernel
\(1_{\ell_i=\ell_j}\) is positive semidefinite, since it is the sum over labels of the rank-one kernels indicating each equivalence class.

It follows that the kernel
\[
 H(a,b)=\log(a+b)-\log\gcd(a,b)
 -1_{\nu_2(a)=\nu_2(b)}\log2 \tag{33}
\]
is conditionally negative semidefinite on positive integers: its first term is conditionally negative semidefinite, while the two subtracted terms are positive semidefinite. Notice also that \(H(a,a)=0\), because
\(\log(2a)=\log a+\log2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. The prime-by-prime opposition construction

Fix a finite set of distinct positive integers \((a_i)_{i\in I}\), and let \(P\) be a finite set of primes containing every prime divisor of every \(a_i+a_j\) with \(i\ne j\). We construct one opposition family for each \(p\in P\).

Write
\[
 v_p(a)=\nu_p(a),\qquad u_p(a)=a/p^{v_p(a)},

a
\]
so \(p\nmid u_p(a)\). Give every positive integer a \(p\)-color as follows.

* If \(p\) is odd, color \(a\) according as the residue of \(u_p(a)\) lies in the lower half \(1,\ldots,(p-1)/2\) or the upper half \((p+1)/2,\ldots,p-1\).
* If \(p=2\), color \(a\) according as the odd number \(u_2(a)\) is \(1\) or \(3\pmod4\).

Let
\[
 \epsilon_p=\begin{cases}1,&p=2,\\0,&p\ne2.\end{cases}

a
\]
If two numbers have the same \(p\)-color, then
\[
 \nu_p(u_p(a)+u_p(b))\le\epsilon_p. \tag{34}
\]
For odd \(p\), two nonzero residues in the same half cannot sum to zero modulo \(p\): residues which sum to \(p\) lie in opposite halves. For \(p=2\), two odd residues with the same class modulo \(4\) have sum congruent to \(2\pmod4\), not \(0\pmod4\). This proves (34).

Define the common baseline
\[
 b_p(a,b)=\min\{v_p(a),v_p(b)\}
 +1_{v_p(a)=v_p(b)}\epsilon_p, \tag{35}
\]
and the adjusted exponents
\[
 x_p(a,b)=v_p(a+b)-b_p(a,b),
\qquad
 y_p(a,b)=v_p(|a-b|)-b_p(a,b) \quad(a\ne b). \tag{36}
\]
These are nonnegative. The minimum valuation always divides both a sum and a difference. If the two valuations are equal and \(p=2\), the two unit parts are odd, so both their sum and difference are even, giving the extra unit in (35). Also, if \(v_p(a)\ne v_p(b)\), then the valuation of \(a+b\) is the smaller valuation, so \(x_p(a,b)=0\). By (34), \(x_p(a,b)=0\) whenever the colors agree.

To build a laminar family, orient the unit part by its color: let
\[
 \widetilde u_p(a)=\begin{cases}u_p(a),&\text{for one color},\\-u_p(a),&\text{for the other color}.
\end{cases}

a
\]
For each level \(n\ge0\), label \(a\) by
\[
 \ell_{p,n}(a)=
 \left(v_p(a),\ \widetilde u_p(a)\bmod p^{n+1+\epsilon_p}\right). \tag{37}
\]
Equality of labels at a higher level implies equality at every lower level, so their equivalence classes form refining partitions and hence a laminar collection. At each level retain only the classes containing both colors. Give each retained class weight \(\log p\). If the same subset occurs at several levels, its weights are added. This produces a finite weighted laminar opposition family after truncating at the maximum valuation of the finitely many pair sums; levels beyond this maximum make no contribution relevant to an opposite-colored pair.

The key point is the interpretation of label equality. If \(a,b\) have opposite colors, their oriented units have opposite signs, so
\[
 \ell_{p,n}(a)=\ell_{p,n}(b)
 \iff v_p(a)=v_p(b)
 \text{ and }p^{n+1+\epsilon_p}\mid u_p(a)+u_p(b)
 \iff n<x_p(a,b). \tag{38}
\]
Moreover, the common label class is automatically bichromatic. Therefore exactly the first \(x_p(a,b)\) levels contribute to opposition. If their colors agree, both opposition and \(x_p(a,b)\) are zero. Thus in every case
\[
 O_p(i,j)=x_p(a_i,a_j)\log p. \tag{39}
\]

For same-colored distinct \(a,b\), equality of labels at level \(n\) means
\(p^{n+1+\epsilon_p}\mid u_p(a)-u_p(b)\), and hence \(n<y_p(a,b)\). Dropping the requirement that the class be bichromatic can only increase the count, so
\[
 A_p(i,j)\le y_p(a_i,a_j)\log p. \tag{40}
\]
For opposite colors the agreement is zero, so (40) remains true. From \(S_p=A_p-O_p\), (36), (39), and (40), the baseline cancels and gives
\[
 S_p(i,j)\le
 \bigl(v_p(|a_i-a_j|)-v_p(a_i+a_j)\bigr)\log p
 \qquad(i\ne j). \tag{41}
\]

We now sum over \(p\in P\). Prime factorization and (35) give
\[
\sum_{p\in P}b_p(a,b)\log p
 =\log\gcd(a,b)+1_{v_2(a)=v_2(b)}\log2. \tag{42}
\]
Here every prime divisor of \(\gcd(a,b)\) belongs to \(P\), since \(\gcd(a,b)\mid a+b\). Also, if the two \(2\)-adic valuations agree, then \(2\mid a+b\), so \(2\in P\). Because all prime divisors of \(a+b\) lie in \(P\), (39), (36), and (42) yield the exact identity
\[
 D(i,j)=\sum_{p\in P}O_p(i,j)=H(a_i,a_j). \tag{43}
\]
It also holds on the diagonal, where both sides are zero. By Section 6, \(D\) is conditionally negative semidefinite.

On the other hand, summing (41) gives
\[
 V(i,j)\le
 \sum_{p\in P}v_p(|a_i-a_j|)\log p-
 \sum_{p\in P}v_p(a_i+a_j)\log p.

a
\]
The second sum is exactly \(\log(a_i+a_j)\), while the first is at most \(\log|a_i-a_j|\), since it is only a partial sum of the nonnegative prime-factorization expansion. Hence
\[
 V(i,j)\le\log|a_i-a_j|-\log(a_i+a_j)<0 \tag{44}
\]
for \(i\ne j\), because the positive integers are distinct and
\(0<|a_i-a_j|<a_i+a_j\).

Thus the hypotheses of the opposition-capacity lemma hold with \(s=|P|\), and we conclude
\[
 |I|\le1024(|P|+1)^8. \tag{45}
\]
Taking \(I=A\) and \(P\) to be precisely the prime support of the pair sums proves the quantitative assertion (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8. Removing zero

The original problem allows subsets of \(\mathbb N\), so zero may occur. For an arbitrary finite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), let \(A^+=A\setminus\{0\}\). Then all elements of \(A^+\) are positive and
\[
 |A|\le|A^+|+1.
\]
Every pair sum from \(A^+\) is also a pair sum from \(A\), so deleting zero cannot enlarge the prime support. Therefore, if \(c(A)=s\), (1) gives
\[
 |A|\le1024(s+1)^8+1. \tag{46}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 9. The extremal function and the limit

For each \(n\), the integer \(f(n)\) in the statement is the minimum of \(c(A)\) over all \(n\)-element finite subsets \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\). This minimum exists because the set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb N\): for example, \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is an admissible set. The defining maximality property says both that \(f(n)\le c(A)\) for every such \(A\), and that every universally valid lower bound is at most \(f(n)\); hence it is exactly this minimum and is attained by some \(A\).

Choose an attaining set \(A\) of cardinality \(n\), so \(c(A)=f(n)\). Applying (46),
\[
 n\le1024(f(n)+1)^8+1. \tag{47}
\]
We finish by deriving the limit from this polynomial inequality.

First, (47) forces \(f(n)\to\infty\). Indeed, if \(f(n)\le b\), then
\[
 n\le1024(b+1)^8+1,
\]
so beyond that fixed bound one must have \(f(n)>b\).

For \(n>0\), since \((f(n)+1)^8\ge1\), (47) implies
\[
 n\le2048(f(n)+1)^8.

a
\]
Taking logarithms gives
\[
 \log n\le\log2048+8\log(f(n)+1). \tag{48}
\]
Because \(f(n)\to\infty\),
\[
 \frac{\log2048}{f(n)}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \frac{\log(f(n)+1)}{f(n)}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Dividing (48) by \(f(n)>0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), we obtain
\[
 0<\frac{\log n}{f(n)}
 \le \frac{\log2048}{f(n)}
 +8\frac{\log(f(n)+1)}{f(n)}\longrightarrow0.

a
\]
Thus \(\log n/f(n)\to0\) through positive values. Taking reciprocals yields
\[
 \frac{f(n)}{\log n}\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
This is exactly the asserted conclusion.
